blocks.text: 7. It is certain that the Hebrews have called the rabbit by this name for some centuries now. Thus Baal Aruch, almost five hundred years ago, under the word תלא אילן thela Aelan, or ilan, says of ferrets: ושמענו שמצויין הן במקומות שצדין בהן שפנים We have heard that they are found in certain places where rabbits are hunted with them. And in R. Isaac, son of Solomon, about one century later, in the book entitled Masal Kadmoni, which contains fables similar to Aesop's, written in bound language, the speakers in the fiftieth fable are השפן והזרזיר, that is, the rabbit and the starling, as the accompanying pictures make plain. And in the Porta coeli, whose author is R. Gersom, tract. 4, ch. 1, fol. 19 d: וקצתם יולידו ולדות רבות כחתול ושפן וארנבת ועכבר And some of them (the animals) produce many young; such as the cat, and the rabbit, and [col. 1003] the hare, and the mouse. And fol. 20 d: ויש מב״ח אשר ביציהם תלוים בכיס ויש מהם שהם דבוקים בבטן כשפן וארנבת וחחול In some animals the testicles hang in a scrotum, but in others they adhere to the belly, as in the rabbit, the hare and the cat. David de Pomis, in his Lexicon: שפן ב״ח או חיה הנקרא קוני״לו בלעז Saphan, an animal, or wild beast, which in the vernacular (that is, Italian) is called Coniglio. And elsewhere: טפז שפן, rabbit, coniglio, animaletto. And again: חגס שפן, rabbit, coniglio. Nor is there any of the Hebrews who interprets it otherwise. 8. Finally, if שפן saphan is the rabbit, it will at once be perfectly clear whence Σπανία [Spania] Spania, or Hispania, took its name. And Σπανία [Spania] will be in Hebrew שפניה, abounding in rabbits. It would have been so called by the Phoenicians because it teems above all with this animal. This we prove at length elsewhere. Hence it is that on a coin of Hadrian, representing Hispania, there is a seated woman with an olive branch in her hand and a rabbit at her feet. From all this, then, it seems to follow that שפן is the rabbit.

Yet three objections can be raised against this interpretation. 1. That rabbits do not ruminate, as is expressly asserted in the Porta coeli, fol. 20 b: אין השפן והארנבת מעלה [II, 411] גרה, The rabbit and the hare do not chew the cud. 2. That they do not live in rocks, but in earthy soil that is easily dug through. 3. That this animal was formerly peculiar to Spain, which is an immense distance from Judaea. Varro, On Agriculture, book 3, chapter 12: There is a third kind, which is born in Spain, in some respects similar to our hare, but low, which they call the rabbit. Pliny, book 8, chapter 55: Of the hare kind also are those which Spain calls rabbits. Aelian, On Animals, book 13, chapter 15: Κόνιλος ὄνομα αὐτῷ [Konilos onoma autō], Its name is conilus (I would prefer κένικλος [keniklos], as in Galen). And a little later: Φυλάττω τὴν ἐπωνυμίαν τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς, ἥνπερ οὖν Ἰβηρίαν Ἑσπέριοι ἔθεντο οἱ πάρος, παρ᾽ οἷς καὶ γίνεταί τε, καὶ ἔστι πάμπολις [Phylattō tēn epōnymian tēn ex archēs, hēnper oun Ibērian Hesperioi ethento hoi paros, par' hois kai ginetai te, kai esti pampolis]. I keep the old Iberian name, which the ancient Spaniards had given it from the beginning, among whom it is both born and most abounds. Galen, book 3 On Foods: Οὐκοῦν ἔτι δεήσομαι λόγων μακρῶν εἰς τὸ τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἔθνος ἐπιχώρια τῶν ζώων ἅπαντα διέρχεσθαι· καθάπερ ἐν Ἰβηρίᾳ τὸ τοῖς λαγωοῖς ὅμοιον ζωΰφιον, ὃ καλοῦσι κένικλον [Oukoun eti deēsomai logōn makrōn eis to ta kath' hekaston ethnos epichōria tōn zōōn hapanta dierchesthai; kathaper en Ibēria to tois lagōois homoion zōyphion, ho kalousi keniklon]. There will be no need of more words to go through all the animals that are peculiar and native to the individual nations: such as in Spain the little animal similar to hares, which they call the rabbit. Since, then, it is established from these passages that the rabbit was a Spanish animal, what need was there to forbid the eating of it to the Jews, to whom it was entirely unknown? ^{(1)}
